Paḍgṛbhi, ‘seizing by the foot,’ is the name in the Rigveda of either a man or a demon. See also paḍbīśa.
Foot notes But it may mean ‘seizing with a cord.’ Cf. Macdonell, Vedic Grammar, p. 34 (top); Pischel, Vedische Studien, 1, 236.
x. 49, 5.
Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 165.

Paḍ-bīśa, the ‘foot-fetter’ of a horse in five passages, two in the Rigveda, and one each in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka upaniṣad, the Chāndogya upaniṣad, and the śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka. Elsewhere its uses are metaphorical. According to Roth, the literal sense is ‘foot-fastening’ (paḍ being = pad, ‘foot,’ and bīśa, written vīśa in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, being connected with the Latin vincire, ‘bind’). Pischel objects that the sense of ‘foot-fastening’ involves the absurdity, in the upaniṣad passages, of a fine horse from the sindhu (Indus) being spoken of as tearing up the peg to which it is fastened. He suggests instead the meaning of ‘hobble,’ which must be right.

He explains the first part of the word as derived from paś, ‘tie.’ Cf. Macdoneli, Vedic Grammar, p. 34 (top). But the form paḍ may be due to a false analogy, and the sense of ‘footfastener’ may express ‘hobble’ quite satisfactorily; it is not confined to a rope tied to a peg in the ground.
